passages.happening:
Gideon and his men camp by the spring of Harod, with the camp of Midian to the north in the valley (verse 1).

Then the LORD says something no general expects. “You have too many people for Me to deliver Midian into their hands, lest Israel glorify themselves over Me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me’” (verse 2).

So Gideon tells anyone who is afraid to go home. Twenty-two thousand leave, and ten thousand stay (verse 3).

“There are still too many people” (verse 4). God tells Gideon to take them down to the water and sift them there. Those who lap the water with their hands to their mouths are set apart from those who kneel to drink. Three hundred lap; all the rest kneel (verses 5-6). “With the three hundred men who lapped the water I will save you and deliver the Midianites into your hand” (verse 7). The rest are sent home, and the three hundred keep their provisions and their rams' horns (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is built on numbers that fall. Thirty-two thousand become ten thousand, and ten thousand become three hundred. God gives the reason at the start, before the first man leaves: so that Israel cannot say, ‘My own hand has saved me’. The danger God names is not defeat. It is pride after victory.

Sending the fearful home was the rule for Israel's army. The law allowed any man who was afraid to return, so that his fear would not spread to others. Gideon himself had been afraid all through chapter 6. Now he watches two out of every three men go home.

The spring of Harod lies at the foot of Mount Gilboa, on the south side of the Jezreel Valley. The hill of Moreh rises on the north side, and the Midianite camp lay between them. Verse 3 speaks of Mount Gilead, which is puzzling, since Gilead is east of the Jordan. Some scholars think it is a copying slip for Gilboa. Others think it was the name of a local hill, or a turn of speech. The text does not settle it.

The word for sifting the men at the water is a word used for refining metal, separating what will be used from the rest.

The test itself is never explained, and that seems to be on purpose. The point is God's choosing, not the men's merit.
passages.later:
The law gave the rule about fear: “Is any man afraid or fainthearted? Let him return home, so that the hearts of his brothers will not melt like his own” (Deuteronomy 20:8). It also warned against the very boast God names here: “You might say in your heart, ‘The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me’” (Deuteronomy 8:17).

A psalm says it plainly: “No king is saved by his vast army; no warrior is delivered by his great strength” (Psalm 33:16). And a prophet: “Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of Hosts” (Zechariah 4:6).
passages.hard:
What was the point of the test at the water? Were the men who lapped the better soldiers?

Readers have long disagreed. One view holds that the three hundred who lapped from their hands stayed alert, watching for danger while they drank, and were the more careful soldiers. Another view notes that the text never says this, and that God's stated purpose was to make the army smaller, not to find the best men. On this reading the test was a way of sorting that showed God's choice. Some even suggest that the lappers were the less disciplined group, which would make the point sharper still.

The text's own weight falls on verses 2 and 7. God will save with three hundred so that Israel cannot boast. Whatever the men were like, the victory is told as God's. A common misreading turns this into a lesson that small, committed teams beat large ones. The chapter's point is that God took Israel's strength away so that the credit could not be theirs.
passages.asks: God sent most of the army home so that no one could boast. Ask where you are tempted to take credit for something God did. And ask what strength you rely on that God might have to take away before you could see him clearly.

passages.t: A dream in the enemy camp
passages.happening:
That night the LORD tells Gideon to attack, for the camp is already given into his hand (verse 9). Then he adds, “But if you are afraid to do so, then go down to the camp with your servant Purah and listen to what they are saying” (verses 10-11).

Gideon goes. The Midianites, the Amalekites and the peoples of the east fill the valley ‘like a swarm of locusts’, with camels ‘as countless as the sand on the seashore’ (verse 12).

He arrives just as a man is telling his friend a dream. A loaf of barley bread came tumbling into the Midianite camp and struck a tent so hard that it fell flat (verse 13). His friend replies, “This is nothing less than the sword of Gideon son of Joash, the Israelite. God has delivered Midian and the whole camp into his hand” (verse 14).

Gideon bows down and worships. He goes back to his men and says, “Get up, for the LORD has delivered the camp of Midian into your hand” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
God knows Gideon is afraid, and this time he offers a sign before Gideon asks for one. He does not shame Gideon for his fear. He sends him to hear something that will strengthen his hands.

In the ancient world dreams were widely taken as messages from the gods, and a man explaining a dream for his friend was a familiar scene. God uses the enemy's own camp to announce the enemy's defeat.

Barley was the cheaper grain, the bread of poor farmers. The tent stood for the Midianites, who lived in tents. The dream pictures a humble Israelite loaf knocking over the raiders' camp. The fear has changed sides.

Notice Gideon's first response. He worships, there in the dark at the edge of the enemy camp, before a single horn is blown.
passages.later:
A psalm remembers this victory as one of God's great acts for his people, and prays for him to do it again: “Make their nobles like Oreb and Zeeb, and all their princes like Zebah and Zalmunna” (Psalm 83:11).

Paul writes of the same way God works: “But God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to shame the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27).
passages.asks: God sent Gideon to overhear the enemy, because he knew Gideon was afraid. Ask how God has met your fear in ways you did not expect. And notice that Gideon worshiped before the battle. Ask whether you thank God for what he has promised, or only for what you have already seen.

passages.happening:
Gideon divides the three hundred into three companies. Each man has a ram's horn in one hand and a clay jar with a torch inside it in the other (verse 16). “Watch me and do as I do” (verse 17). When Gideon blows his horn, they are all to blow theirs from all around the camp and shout, “For the LORD and for Gideon!” (verse 18).

They reach the edge of the camp at the start of the middle watch, just after the guard has changed. They blow the horns and smash the jars, and they shout, “A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!” (verses 19-20). Each man stands in his place around the camp, and the whole Midianite army runs, crying out as it goes (verse 21). The LORD sets the men in the camp against one another with their swords, and they flee toward the Jordan (verse 22).

Men of Naphtali, Asher and Manasseh join the chase (verse 23). Gideon calls on Ephraim to seize the fords of the Jordan ahead of the fleeing army (verse 24). They capture the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb, kill them, and bring their heads to Gideon across the Jordan (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The night was divided into watches, three in the Old Testament, and the middle watch began around ten at night. Striking just after the guard changed meant new sentries whose eyes had not yet grown used to the dark, and a camp asleep.

Normally only a few men in an army carried horns, to give signals to the rest. Three hundred horns sounding from every side would make a sleeping camp believe a vast army had surrounded it. The crash of breaking jars and three hundred sudden lights in the darkness did the rest.

The battle is told as sound and light, not as combat. The only swords that strike are Midianite swords, turned on one another. Israel's three hundred stand still, each man in his place.

The horns recall Jericho, where the walls fell at the sound of rams' horns and a shout, not at a blow from a sword.

The battle cry joins God and his servant: ‘A sword for the LORD and for Gideon’. The order matters, God first. In the next chapter Gideon will begin to take more of the credit for himself.

The fleeing army made for the fords of the Jordan, the way home to the desert. Gideon cuts them off by calling Ephraim, as Ehud's men had once held the fords against Moab. Ephraim is called in late, and that will cause trouble in the next chapter. Oreb and Zeeb mean raven and wolf. The bringing of their heads is the grim custom of ancient war, told without comment.
passages.later:
The story of the horns recalls the fall of Jericho: “So when the rams’ horns sounded, the people shouted” (Joshua 6:20).

Isaiah remembers the place where Oreb fell: “as when He struck Midian at the rock of Oreb” (Isaiah 10:26). And he speaks of a coming rescue in the same terms: “For as in the day of Midian You have shattered the yoke of their burden” (Isaiah 9:4).
passages.asks: Three hundred men stood still, each in his place, and God did the rest. Ask whether you can hold your place faithfully when the outcome is not in your hands. And notice the cry, ‘For the LORD and for Gideon’. Ask how much of the credit for what God does through you you want for yourself.
